title: Estius: man was made free, lord of things and God's friend, so no harm could befall him in God's friendship
source_text: IX. Ad cujus rei intelligentiam monet hominem non esse a Deo institutum ut creaturam mere servilem, sicut instituta est brutorum natura, quae proinde naturaliter & morti sunt obnoxia, & pro utilitate hominum occidi possunt: imo & alia aliis per mortem in usum nutrimenti cedunt: sed Deum fecisse hominem, perinde ut angelos, natura sua liberum, & aliarum rerum Dominum, atque insuper ipsius Dei per gratiam & justitiam velut socium & amicum. Indeque satis intelligi sic hominem institutum esse, ut ei nihil adversum accideret, quamdiu in Dei amicitia permaneret: sed futurum ut semper juncta essent, seque invicem consequerentur haec duo: bonum esse & beatum esse: itemque innocentem esse & expertem esse miseriae. Et hanc legem ita esse perpetuam, sic justitia divina postulante, ut ea sublata ordo universi deformaretur.
pass_a_gloss: For understanding which matter he warns that man was not instituted by God as a merely servile creature, as the nature of brutes was instituted, which therefore are naturally also liable to death, and can be killed for the utility of men: nay, and some yield to others through death for the use of nourishment: but that God made man, just like the angels, free by his nature, and lord of other things, and moreover through grace and justice as it were the companion and friend of God himself. And hence it is sufficiently understood that man was so instituted, that nothing adverse would befall him, as long as he remained in God's friendship: but that it would be that these two would always be joined, and would follow each other: to be good and to be blessed: and likewise to be innocent and to be free of misery. And that this law is so perpetual, divine justice so demanding, that if it were taken away the order of the universe would be deformed.
pass_b_english: To explain this, he points out that God did not make man a merely servile creature, as he made the nature of the brutes. They are therefore naturally subject to death and may be killed for men's use; indeed, some of them give way to others by death to serve as food. God made man, like the angels, free by nature and lord of other things, and besides that, through grace and righteousness, a kind of companion and friend of God himself.

From this, he says, it is clear enough that man was so made that nothing hostile would befall him as long as he remained in God's friendship. Two pairs would always go together and follow from each other: being good and being happy, and likewise being innocent and being free of misery.
And this law is so permanent, because divine justice requires it, that if it were removed the order of the universe would be disfigured.

choices.english: a kind of companion and friend
choices.why: Velut softens the claim; 'a kind of' keeps that hedge.
